emulatedHibernation.note: Orange emulates hibernation. When an object with open accepted WebSockets is idle, Orange drops the object and keeps its sockets open, and the next message or alarm builds the object again. The Rivet actor stays running the whole time, so the memory and the cost of each connected object remain. This is not Cloudflare's hibernation, where a hibernated object uses no memory and is not billed for duration. An emulated result shows what a step does when the sleep check also accepts this state as asleep. It never changes the status of a step or a claim. A project that fails only hibernation steps, and passes them all this way, shows as works, with emulated hibernation, and is counted apart from the projects that work.

failedSteps.label: WebSocket hibernation not available on Rivet 3

notices.title: WebSocket hibernation
notices.cloudflare: A socket stays open while the object sleeps, and a message wakes the object.
notices.orange: Orange emulates hibernation, and real hibernation is coming soon. When an object with an open accepted WebSocket is idle, Orange drops the object and its in-memory state and keeps the socket open. The next message builds a new instance of the object. The Rivet actor stays running the whole time, and it sleeps once the last socket closes. A client stays connected, but the actor does not sleep while it does.
notices.why: Rivet 3 has paused WebSocket hibernation, so an actor cannot sleep with a socket open. Orange hibernates the object inside the running actor instead.
notices.action: Have clients reconnect on any close, and don't depend on one close code. Keep anything that must survive hibernation or a restart in storage. Close sockets you no longer need, so the actor can sleep.
drawbacks: An object with an open socket is always a running actor and does not scale to zero: the actor, its sockets, and their state stay in memory. Before the emulation, an idle awake object cost about 1.1 MB in total, in Orange and the Engine, and each idle socket on one object cost about 0.2 MB. About half of an object's cost stayed after it slept. Measured through `orange serve` on one machine, with 1,000 idle objects or 1,000 idle sockets on one object, and not measured again with the emulation. It is not a limit.

A deploy closes open sockets. On one cluster, each client reconnected on the first try: `1012` on 4 sockets and `1011` on 1. The object is a new instance, and storage survives. In-memory state and the old sockets do not. Whether the object gets `webSocketClose` during a rollout is not measured.
Old and new runners overlap for about 100 s during a rollout, and the Engine can place new objects on the old runner then. Those clients get cut off soon after opening.
Under `orange dev`, a restart closes open sockets with `1012` and a crash with `1006`. In both cases a reconnect works and storage survives.

Orange pings every network socket every 30 s, because Cloudflare closes idle sockets on pool URLs at 125 s with `1006`. With pings, idle sockets stayed open until a rollout closed them at 695 s. A Worker and its objects never see the pings. `wrangler dev` kept idle sockets open for 360 s with no pings. Real Cloudflare is not measured: its docs say idle sockets get closed and recommend a heartbeat.

A client whose connection is cut gives the object `webSocketClose` with `1006` within about 1 s. A client that stays connected but stops answering pings is closed with `1006` at about 90 s. The object sleeps after both.
`webSocketClose` gets `1001 "gateway disconnected"` where a client closed cleanly with `1000`. `wrangler dev` passes the client's code.

The object hibernates, but its actor does not sleep with a socket open. Real projects' steps that wait for every actor to sleep fail with `Some actor was still awake`. The real-project results show each of those steps again under a sleep check that also accepts the emulation.

claims.title: Inbound email: `email()`, `forward()`, and `reply()`
claims.cloudflare: Email Routing delivers mail to the `email()` handler, and `message.forward()` and `message.reply()` send it on.
claims.orange: A message POSTed to `/cdn-cgi/handler/email` runs `email()`: raw MIME, or a SendGrid or Mailgun inbound webhook. `forward()` and `reply()` send through `ORANGE_EMAIL_SMTP_URL`, and `setReject()` answers 400. With `ORANGE_EMAIL_INBOUND_SECRET` set, a wrong secret gets 401 and `email()` does not run. `orange serve` serves the route only when the secret is set. The evidence here runs on `orange dev`.
claims.why: Email Routing itself, Cloudflare's MX and routing rules, is Cloudflare-only. Orange has no mail server, so something else must receive the mail and POST it.

notes: Six projects also ran on Rivet Cloud, one run each on a Free cluster. These results are separate from the local ones above.

Each scenario ran on one shared Free cluster, recorded as Engine 3.0.0 when it was created, the day before these runs. That version comes from the creation record, and was not read during the runs. Each project then got its own Free cluster, where one real request proved it. Those clusters report Engine 3.0.0.
Only `starbasedb` used `orange deploy`'s upload and rollout. The others used the image `orange deploy --dry-run` writes, uploaded and rolled out with the Rivet CLI.

Sleep isn't proven on a pool. The Engine API's actor timestamps are null, and these images log no lifecycle lines, so sleep steps wait past the idle window and read state afterward. A restart step is a real rollout to a newly built image.
A deploy reports done before the new build serves, so each scenario waited for the old node to leave and a project-specific request to succeed.
The Orange under test was a local merge of the CLI and Durable Object branches, before they landed.

projects.what: A SQL database over HTTP and WebSocket, built on a Durable Object's SQLite.
projects.ran: The API refused a request with no token. A client created a table, inserted rows, ran a transaction, used the REST API and JSON export, and queried over a WebSocket. The table survived an idle wait and a real rollout.
shortfalls: The cron callback step did not apply: it calls a local server, which a pool can't reach.

The recorded run is the third attempt. The first was stopped because the old build might still have been serving. The second failed on rows the first had left and on a wrong sleep check in the test runner.
The API needs a token, and there is no page to open in a browser.

projects.what: The sync backend of tldraw's multiplayer whiteboard, with one Durable Object per room and assets in R2.
projects.ran: Assets uploaded to and read from R2 on a Google Cloud Storage bucket, through Orange's S3 settings. Two clients synced pages over WebSockets, a late joiner got them, and a page survived the room emptying and a real rollout.
shortfalls: This is the backend only, with no editor to open.
The image needed the Worker bundled by hand first, because the Orange it ran on could not install `workspace:` packages inside the image.
Only the object reads and writes the project uses ran against Cloud Storage.

projects.what: A workspace in a Durable Object, with a filesystem and a shell that runs in a Dynamic Worker. This was the first Dynamic Worker on a cluster.
projects.ran: Files written through the object read back, each workspace stayed separate, and a shell in a Dynamic Worker read and wrote the same files. A bundled skill mounted read-only. Files survived an idle wait and a real rollout.
shortfalls: The image needed the Worker bundled by hand first, because the project's package comes from its monorepo.
The scenario does not touch the R2 mount. A separate check read and listed a Cloud Storage object through it. The project's mount is read-only.

projects.what: A status page for the Kody app, where a one-minute cron probes components and a Durable Object stores incidents.
projects.ran: The page and its JSON read from the store. The real cron fired on the pool, and three failing passes opened an incident, which survived an idle wait and a real rollout.
shortfalls: Its origin points at a host that never answers, so the pool doesn't probe the project's real site. So every component reads down, and that outage comes from this setup.
Two steps did not apply, because they need an origin that answers or recovers.
Operator alert email needs a real credential.
A binding to the project's jobs Worker points at a Worker that isn't deployed. No step called it.

projects.what: A collaborative text editor fixture on PartyServer, with Yjs documents in Durable Objects.
projects.ran: Two editors synced edits both ways over WebSockets, and a custom message reached the others. A document was saved when its room emptied, came back after an idle wait, stayed separate from another room's, and survived a real rollout.
shortfalls: Editors staying connected across a room's hibernation failed, as expected: WebSocket hibernation is not available on Rivet 3, so open sockets keep the object awake.
The editor client isn't in the deployed assets, so there is nothing to open in a browser.

projects.what: Supermemory's MCP server, which gives AI clients a memory, with a Durable Object for each user's active space and for upload sessions.
projects.ran: The server described itself and its OAuth metadata, refused a client with no token, and refused an unknown upload token. With a real Supermemory sign-in, a token was accepted on the pool, an upload session worked once and refused a second use, and the active space carried across connections.
shortfalls: Uploads don't work for a real client on a pool URL. The Worker builds its upload URL from `MCP_RESOURCE`, which stays on Supermemory's production host so that tokens match, so a client following it gets a 401 from production. The passing step posted the same path to the pool by hand.
The image needed `build.command` removed after running it by hand, because the Orange it ran on refused a custom build.
The sign-in step ran by a separate script, after two attempts stopped on that script's own checks.

steps.name: serves the server description and the OAuth resource metadata
an MCP client without a token gets 401 with the resource metadata
SpaceState refuses an upload token with no session
the active space is stored in SpaceState and an upload session is consumed once
steps.note: Ran once with a real Supermemory sign-in, by a separate script through the project's public MCP API. The upload went to the pool by hand, because the Worker advertises Supermemory's production host for uploads.
